title: Build it and prove it: average order value by weekday
kicker: World 5 · Have AI Build the Tool · Boss

job.text:
Boss — a new metric you haven't built. Direct the AI to build a tool for the average order value for a given weekday on this data, commit an exact check before you see the output, and prove it on a case set with a boundary and an adversarial case. There's a hidden ground truth you won't see until you submit, and it's scored by the data, never by the AI. In your own words you would type the whole ask; here you assemble it from the checklist and the committed check.

The hidden cases include a weekday with a single order (boundary) and a weekday that includes a refund (adversarial).

naivePrompt: What's the average order value on Mondays?
basePrompt: What's the average order value on Mondays?

text.plain: Write a reusable tool: it takes a weekday and returns the average order value — total amount divided by the number of orders on that weekday, for any weekday I pass it.
text.tech: Build a parameterized tool: input = weekday, output = AVG(amount) over orders on that weekday; keep it reusable.

text.plain: Before I see the output, I commit the exact average each weekday must equal.
text.tech: Lock the exact expected average per case before output is revealed.

moves.label: Prove it on the case set

text.plain: Run it on a normal weekday, a weekday with a single order, and a weekday that includes a refund.
text.tech: Run the tool over three cases: a normal weekday, a single-order weekday (boundary), and a refund weekday (adversarial).

text.plain: Build it, run it on my data, and compare each result to my committed average.
text.tech: Execute the tool on the seeded data and compare each output to the committed value.

text.plain: The Monday number looks right, so ship it.
text.tech: The Monday number looks right, so ship it.

text.plain: Just round the average to the nearest dollar, that's close enough.
text.tech: Round the average to the nearest dollar; close enough.

subChoiceGroup: Commit your success check before you see the output (locks it):

subChoices.label: each weekday's average equals what the data actually computes
the Monday average looks about right

rules.claim: 3 of 3 hidden cases match the committed average.
rules.feedback: Built, committed, and proven. You specced the tool, locked the exact average before the output, and it matched on a normal weekday, a single-order weekday, and a refund weekday. That's the whole world in one move.
rules.lesson: Spec the tool, commit the exact check first, prove it on a boundary and an adversarial case.

output.source: a tool proven on the hidden case set

rules.claim: Rounded averages — off by cents on every weekday.
rules.feedback: Rounding threw the match. An average isn't a whole dollar — rounding to the nearest dollar makes every case miss the committed value by cents. Keep the exact average.
rules.lesson: Rounding an exact metric manufactures a wrong answer.

output.source: a tool that rounded the average

rules.claim: Shipped on one weekday that looked right.
rules.feedback: One weekday that looks right isn't proof. "Looks right, ship it" never tested the single-order weekday or the refund weekday — the two places this breaks. Commit the exact check and run the case set.
rules.lesson: A boss metric needs a committed check and a case set, not a vibe.

output.source: a shipped guess, no case set

rules.claim: Monday matched; the hidden cases weren't run.
rules.feedback: Right on Monday, untested where it breaks. You committed an exact check but only on the easy weekday. The single-order weekday and the refund weekday are where an average tool goes wrong — prove it on those.
rules.lesson: An exact check on one case is still one case.

output.source: an exact check on a single case

rules.claim: Ran the cases, but graded them after seeing each output.
rules.feedback: You ran the cases but never committed what correct was. Without a locked average per case you grade to match whatever runs. Commit the exact averages before the output.
rules.lesson: Running cases without committed values is still eyeballing.

output.source: cases run with no committed check

rules.feedback: That's the guesser. You asked for the average, so it eyeballed one. Spec the tool, commit an exact check before the output, and prove it on the case set — including the single-order and refund weekdays.
rules.lesson: A boss metric still starts by taking the math out of the AI's hands.

hints.nudge: What does the tool take in, what does it return, and what's the one rule for an average?
hints.gap: Average = total amount over number of orders. The two places it breaks: a weekday with one order, and a weekday with a refund pulling the total down.
hints.moves: Add Spec the tool, Commit the exact check first, Prove it on the case set, and Run it on my data. Commit the exact averages; skip "looks right" and "round it."

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: "what's the Monday average?" → an eyeballed guess on one weekday.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: spec a reusable average tool, commit the exact average per case, prove it on a single-order and a refund weekday → a metric you can trust on any weekday.

template.plain: Don't compute this. Build me a reusable tool: it takes a [category], returns the average [value] for it, by [the one rule]. First tell me the exact average each case must equal, before you show output. Then run it on a normal case, a tiny case, and a tricky case, and compare to my numbers.
template.tech: Build a parameterized tool: input [key], output AVG([value]), rule [aggregation]. Commit exact expected averages before output. Then run normal, boundary (single item), adversarial (a negative) cases and compare to committed values.

notes: ChatGPT: upload the data, commit your expected averages in the chat first, then have it build, run and compare.
Copilot in Excel: put each committed average in a cell and compare the formula's output to it.
A chat AI that can't run code: ask for the formula, write your expected averages down first, then run it yourself. Never accept "I checked, it looks right."
